summary: A research group document on using network coding in and above the network layer in satellite communication systems. It aims to encourage wider deployment of these techniques and identifies open research issues. It is informational and not a protocol standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Satellite links lose or delay data. This explores clever ways of mixing data pieces together so lost pieces can be rebuilt.

questions: how does network coding help with packet loss
subtitle: Using clever data mixing to recover from satellite link losses

tldr.problem: Satellite links suffer from packet loss due to residual errors, long round-trip delays (over 0.7 seconds for geostationary satellites), and unstable channel conditions. Retransmissions over these links add unacceptable delays to end-user experience.
tldr.mechanism: Network coding creates repair packets by taking linear combinations of lost or damaged packets. Instead of retransmitting the exact original packets, routers send encoded packets from which receivers can recover missing data.
tldr.outcome: Network coding is a research technique that has not yet seen widespread commercial deployment in satellite systems but offers promising benefits in scenarios like relay channels, multicast, hybrid terrestrial-satellite access, and dealing with variable channel conditions.

today: RFC 8975 is an Informational report from the Coding for Efficient Network Communications Research Group (NWCRG) of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). It is not a standard or formal protocol specification but rather a survey of where network coding could improve satellite communications. The technique remains largely a research topic, with limited commercial deployment to date.

sections.title: The Satellite Problem and Network Coding
sections.content:
Satellite communication systems (SATCOM) serve broadcast, point-to-point, and Internet-of-Things applications. Traditional physical and link-layer error correction handles most errors, but residual packet losses still occur. The real problem is long round-trip delay: geostationary satellites have delays exceeding 0.7 seconds. When a packet is lost, retransmitting it over this link adds significant delay, degrading user experience and wasting expensive satellite capacity.

Network coding offers an alternative. Rather than retransmit original packets, a router can send an encoded repair packet—a linear combination of lost or damaged packets. Receivers that have heard some packets can decode the missing ones by listening to the repair packet. This technique can be applied at the application, transport, or network layer and offers benefits in multiple SATCOM scenarios.

While the research community has done substantial work on network coding, commercial SATCOM systems have not yet widely adopted it. This document identifies opportunities for wider deployment and open research challenges.
sections.plainLanguage: When a satellite packet gets lost, instead of waiting and resending it, you can send a coded packet that combines several original packets. Receivers can extract the lost packet from the coded one.

sections.title: Use Cases Where Coding Helps
sections.content:
The RFC identifies six main scenarios where network coding improves SATCOM performance. In a two-way relay channel, two satellite terminals send packets to a server, which codes them together and sends a single combined packet. This saves capacity compared to sending two separate flows.

Reliable multicast sends a multicast flow to multiple terminals. When different terminals lose different packets, a coding server can send a single repair packet that recovers losses at multiple terminals simultaneously. This is more efficient than traditional approaches like NORM and FLUTE, which are limited to block coding and cannot decode before receiving a complete block.

Hybrid access combines satellite, DSL, and LTE links to give users redundant paths. Network coding at the transport layer can recover from losses on any path, improving tolerance for packet reordering when links have very different round-trip times.

In LAN losses, a lossy WiFi link between a user and a satellite terminal creates an end-to-end problem. Network coding at the terminal prevents end-to-end retransmissions. When channel conditions vary rapidly (in Q/V bands or with mobile users), physical layer adaptation may not keep pace, leaving packet losses. Coding provides a second recovery mechanism.

Finally, gateway handover switching between satellite gateways can lose packets if gateways are not synchronized. Network coding during handover improves reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Coding helps when two terminals send data, when one satellite sends the same data to many users, when users have multiple links, when WiFi is lossy, when channels change, and when switching between ground stations.

sections.title: Implementation Layers and Coding Approaches
sections.content:
Network coding can be implemented at different layers. Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) operates above the link layer and targets packet-loss recovery. The document focuses on linear network coding techniques—where repair packets are linear combinations of original packets—and excludes content coding (like video compression) and other non-linear operations.

Coding can use a single-path approach where one flow is coded, or inter-flow coding where repair packets combine multiple flows. Inter-flow coding is more efficient but riskier: a single corrupted repair packet can affect multiple flows.

A typical SATCOM architecture includes satellite ground gateways with network, access, and physical gateway functions. Network coding operations can be placed at application servers, gateways, or satellite terminals depending on the use case. The document emphasizes that coding can also be implemented as Virtual Network Functions (VNFs) in virtualized network infrastructure, which will become important as 5G and next-generation SATCOM systems adopt Network Function Virtualization.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add coding at different points in the network: near the application, at gateways, or at terminals. The choice depends on what you are trying to fix.

sections.title: Open Research Questions
sections.content:
Several challenges remain before network coding can be widely deployed in SATCOM. First, interaction with congestion control: SATCOM systems often use Performance Enhancing Proxies (PEPs) that limit the impact of long delays on Internet protocols. Adding coding to a PEP raises questions about how the two mechanisms interact and whether coding helps or hurts overall performance.

Second, resource optimization: deciding how much redundancy to add (coding overhead) to balance Quality of Experience against satellite capacity usage is a difficult trade-off. Satellite resources are expensive and must be used efficiently.

Third, virtualized infrastructure: as SATCOM systems shift toward virtual network functions and cloud-native architectures, network coding must integrate with service function chaining and virtualized gateways, all while managing limited buffer capacities.

Finally, delay-tolerant networks (DTN): deep-space communications have extremely long delays and frequent disruptions. Network coding with adaptive re-encoding could enable reliable E2E communication over DTN, but integration with the IETF DTN stack is an open question. The CCSDS (space systems) community has defined packet erasure coding for their architecture, but bridging to IETF standards remains undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: Before satellites use coding widely, research needs to answer: does it help when combined with other optimizations, how much coding overhead should be added, how does it work in virtual networks, and how does it work for deep-space missions.
